Interlude: Anke

Royal Treasurer Anke Lohman was having a good day. It had started excellently when she had managed to intercept several accounting ledgers incorrectly addressed to Royal Secretary Jolanda Vos, who in yet another instance of gross overreach was again attempting to usurp Anke's position as treasurer for Princess Marcelle. She knew the younger elf would have something venomous to say, and might even come to her office and start complaining, but 'workplace drama'—as Princess Marcelle put it—was the highest form of politics, and Anke relished the cut and thrust. Although inexperienced, Jolanda had a ruthless quality that Anke could respect, and Anke was big enough of a woman to admit that Jolanda was far, far better at sucking up to the boss than Anke had ever been.

The day had only gotten better when Princess Marcelle had personally requested her help to bind a language spirit. Although their previous status of equals—and thus in competition with one another—had made for a somewhat shaky foundation of their new boss-employee relationship, Anke had managed to salvage the situation, and Princess Marcelle didn't seem to hold it against her. Or, perhaps, Anke had managed to make herself useful enough that the powerful fairy had decided to let it slide. Regardless, a victory.

"Not like that, Princess," said Anke, shaking her head as Princess Marcelle practised casting a binding. "You don't want to choke the life out of the spirit—it needs to have some flex in it, so that the spirit can make its demands known; you need an agreement, otherwise you'll always have to focus on maintaining the link."

Princess Marcelle scowled, but cast the spell again, this time not so crushingly potent.

"Wonderful! You're such a skilled wizard, Princess!"

"Stop that Anke, it's fucking creepy," said Princess Marcelle.

"What is, my lady?" asked Anke, furrowing her brows and placing a hand on Princess Marcelle's arm.

"You being nice, also calling me 'my lady' and 'Princess'—cut it out," said Princess Marcelle, jerking her arm away. "OK, are we ready to bind this thing?"

"I—ah—believe so," said Anke, cursing herself for coming on too strong.

Flattery of one's boss was important, but there was a fine line to tread, and every boss was different: some loved sycophancy, others wanted you to act more independent; some liked flattery and flirtation, others, like Princess Marcelle, got creeped out by it. Anke would need to re-calibrate her efforts; perhaps consult the literature.

"Alright," said the Princess, doing one last check over of the brassy runic array before spreading her hands and pushing magic into the runes.

The symbols lit up, dancing with icy blue and verdant green as the ritual began.

"And I really have to read the stupid poem?" said Princess Marcelle.

"Yes, your highness," said Anke, toning down the 'suck up' a little bit.

Princess Marcelle sighed. "'Sprite hear this writ, one quick of wit,'" she began, reading the scrap of paper. "'A sprite wise do I seek for pact, to translate tongues that I do lack!'"

Nothing happened.

"You need to really mean it, your highness," said Anke.

"Firstly, don't call me that either," said Princess Marcelle. "And secondly, this is… very stupid magic. And thirdly, pact doesn't rhyme with lack."

"That's deliberate, your majesty," said Anke.

"Don't call me that either."

"The language spirit we're trying to summon will be annoyed at the incorrect rhyme, and want to come and correct you," said Anke.

Princess Marcelle sighed and repeated the spell. This time there was a flare of magic in the centre, and a tiny ball of viridian light coalesced.

"That doesn't rhyme!" said the amorphous ball of light. "Stupid! Stupid!"

"Got you here though," said Marci, looking back at the book she had borrowed from Anke. "Alright, dammit… I offer you a pact? For you to answer my calls to translate languages for me?"

"Hmm…" said the sprite. "Terms?"

"I'll give you…" Marci furrowed her brow. "'A quill, a bottle of ink, and a scrap of parchment?' That's a fucking awful deal."

"Shh!" said Anke. "Don't tell it that!"

"Bad deal?" said the stupid language sprite. "No! We don't want a bad deal! We want… we want twice as much! Two quills! Two bottles of Ink! Two scraps of parchment!"

"Sure," said Princess Marcelle with a shrug, not even attempting to haggle.

"Marci!" gasped Anke, momentarily forgetting her employer's rank. "You're— you're distorting the sprite labour market! It's going to tell all the other sprites, and increase the price for everyone!"

Princess Marcelle made a gesture very unbecoming of her station, and Anke had to fight the urge to tell off her boss for her reckless over-payment as the small, beautiful, but worryingly un-economically savvy fairy sealed the pact.

***

Testimony

Ullholm was abuzz with activity. Not in the upper, demon quarter, where the ruling class of Callum's empire were hunkered down in their manors and apartments, but on the streets, in the canteens, and in the large open-air debates that were taking part.

Kattdjur, as well as Kanindjen, Hunddar, and Musdir, had arrived from all across Callum's domain, representatives appointed by people of towns, farms, plantations, mines, foundries, vineyards, river ports, and many more. They were here for the Constitutional Convention, where the rules and basic laws of the People's Republic of Kattlandia would be laid down.

The Dreadfort was already on its way north, having left Krefeld an Nain in the early morning a week after Callum's defeat. She had kept the Dark Bulwark where it was after transferring its immense treasury and a huge chunk of its supplies and troops to the Dreadfort. Her reasoning wasn't, despite what some of the journals in Krefeld had claimed, a desire to intimidate, but rather that because of the portal that Callum had established in Ullholm, it gave her a way to rapidly transfer troops directly between Dark Bulwark and the North without needing them to go through the Underworld's portal Nexus—something that would doubtlessly be noticed by not only the Infernal Council, but also her enemy Shardkeepers.

Beyond angry letters, Marci hadn't heard much from the other Shardkeepers. None of them had so much as come near the borders of Kattlandia—something she had been extremely worried about. She knew that wouldn't last forever, that their fear of Marci's unknown power wouldn't stay their hands indefinitely, but she was glad that their unbalanced, fearful posture gave her longer to prepare for the inevitable war.

That upcoming war, and how it might be won, was why she was sitting at a desk in front of a council of thirty men and women. They were in Callum's throne room; although the gilded seat had been stripped of its gold and gems and then burnt in the main courtyard. Some of the pomp had been left, although the purple and black banners had been replaced with the pink and white that had been the traditional colours of Kattlandia.

Now, rather than a throne and no other furniture, it had dozens of slightly irregular tables that had been dragged in to form a semi-circle for the elected delegates of the constitutional committee, a long desk facing them for those they summoned to speak before them, and which was where Marci was currently sitting, with Olaf, Anke, Rafferty, Saoirse, Jolanda and an annoyed Likes-Hammers (who would 'much rather be workings!') behind her.

There were also benches further back where members of the Kattlandian public, including a where few journalists from the remarkably quickly put together journals and newspapers were sitting, waiting to report on the meeting to the wider public.

"I call this committee inquest to order," said a grey-haired kattdjur woman, Toren Lundin, banging her gavel.

Toren Lundin had been elected chair of the committee that would draft the constitution over the course of the next week or two and then put it to the people. She was dressed, like all the kattdjur, quite simply in what had probably been her work uniform, in a pair of blue overalls and a worn but very clean collared shirt. She had scars visible on her hands, and around the back of her neck that Marci had seen when she'd limped in with the help of a cane to take her seat. Tokens, no doubt, of the overseers who had once ruled her days.

"We are here to question Shardkeeper Marcelle du Valmont, and make provisional recommendations based on her testimony for the defence of the Republic," continued Ms. Lundin. "The Shardkeeper has requested a brief opening statement, and unless there is objection we will now hear it?"

She was speaking in Kattdjur, which was a language that Marci had only the faintest of grasps over, but which was intelligible to her thanks to the language sprite she had gotten Anke to show her how to summon and make a bargain with. It wasn't proper wizardry, but Marci did have to admit that the not particularly intelligent sprite who she'd bargained for the help of with a few items was useful.

Sprites were a kind of spirit, the more simple ones, related distantly to beings of incredible complexity like Aegis—although Aegis had been made artificially by mind-bogglingly advanced wizardry. Most were natural, and formed in places with symbolic significance—language sprites tended to form in libraries and the like, and were harmless, content to just absorb written and spoken language.

Bargaining with sprites or spirits or elementals or fey or whatever else was considered 'not really proper spellcraft' by most wizards, and undergraduates were banned from using language sprites specifically because they were crutches that stopped people actually learning languages themselves, or learning the more reliable translation spells that were more work, but produced better results. Marci, however, was no longer an undergraduate, and didn't have the time to become fluent in Kattdjur, so she had decided to lower herself to making a contract with the simple being.

There was a moment of somewhat confused discussion amongst the representatives as they processed the Chairwoman's words, some of whom seemed very overwhelmed by their positions, others carrying the immense responsibility with more grace. All of them, however, in marked contrast to the Kaiser's Court and the Infernal Council she had been recently dealing with, betrayed no open hostility towards her. There were uneasy looks at Rafferty and Saoirse, although the fact they knew the pair were part of Marci's inner circle who had helped put an end to their slaving overlord, Callum, made the dislike more muted than it might have otherwise been. Hopefully, this wouldn't want to make her claw out her like the other two meetings had.

"No?" said Ms. Lundin. "Good. Then you have the floor, Ms. Du Valmont."

Marci cleared her throat and tried to settler her nerves—strangely, this was almost as bad as when she'd come to speak to the Infernal Council. Different, in that here she wanted these people to like her, not fear her, but daunting all the same. She'd never admit it, least of all to her mother, but she supposed all those public speaking classes she'd been made to take growing up were good for something.

"Thank-you, Chairwoman," she said. "And thank-you to the committee for agreeing to speak with me. Before we get into any details, I first wanted to make a few things clear. Firstly, I have no intention of ruling the Republic, or interfering in your self-governance in any way. I am not Callum with blue hair and wings; I am not, and will never be a tyrant."

There was a smattering of applause from the gallery, but Ms. Lundin banged her gavel angrily. "Order! We are not a circus!"

"Second, I am acutely aware that I possess an immense treasury claimed from Callum that was extracted from the blood, sweat, and tears of Kattlandia. It is my intention to return this to the Republic."

This time, Ms. Lundin wasn't able to contain the eruption of applause, and even the Committee got involved. Marci blushed, although she was happy to be so well received, it felt slightly perverse that just doing the right thing was seen as such a monumentally kind and exceptional act.

"Thirdly, although I will not rule it, it is my intention to defend the Republic from the other Shardkeepers," said Marci. "Already the Dreadfort is on its way here, carrying with it ten thousand troops and the weaponry that brought Callum down, as well as the treasury I will be returning to the people of Kattlandia."

More applause, which the Chairwoman allowed to continue for a while before banging her gavel and demanding order once again.

"That is a summary of my basic intent and immediate plans," said Marci. "Although there are several important details that we will need to go over. Thank-you, Madam Chairwoman. I cede the floor."

"Very good, thank-you Ms. Du Valmont," said the elderly Kattdjur woman. "In that case, I welcome questions from the committee… Citizen Gustav Ehrling, I believe you were first?"

A young, sharp green eyed and green haired Kattdjur man stood up. "Thank-you Madam Chairwoman," he said in a smooth voice that set Marci slightly on edge. A politician, this one. "And thank-you, Shardkeeper; I think I speak for all of us when I offer to you the Republic's eternal thanks for your heroic actions on our behalf, and to you, Marshall Havström—it heartens me to know that those who managed to escape the calamity did not forget their homeland."

Olaf, who had been acting a bit weird for the past two days that they had been in the capital of the new Republic, nodded, but didn't say anything.

Marci wanted to interject that Rafferty had also been indispensable in Callum's defeat, but she knew that she didn't have the floor. And it was one thing to flout the customs of a bunch of stupid, vapid nobles or psychopathic demon warlords, but Marci had far more respect for the meeting decorum of this new Republic than those vicious institutions. This would, at least hopefully, be a government worthy of the name.

"My question concerns the rest of the Northlands," said Gustav Ehrling. "What are your intentions regarding the other Shardkeepers? Do you intend to take the fight to them? Liberate all of our fellow Northerners locked in chains, Ms. Du Valmont?"

There was a flurry of whispers from the gallery, and Marci pursed her lips. She understood, from a public facing point of view, why he would ask such a thing—the desire to overthrow all the Shardkeepers and liberate the entire Northlands was a popular one in the nascent Republic, and which she had heard regularly in the public debates she had listened in on. It was Marci's intention to, even.

But there was no way in the Hells that she could say that publicly. News of what was said here would get back to the other Shardkeepers, and if Marci announced that she planned to kill them all, they would unify and overwhelm her—ancient Superweapon or not. There were efforts to identify agents of other Shardkeepers, Marci leading the way with them even, but there were a lot of people to get through, and her spells only checked for Shardbonds, not more conventional spies.

So much for her hopes that this meeting wouldn't also be a train-wreck.

"Mr. Ehrling, yes?" said Marci, peering at the chalk-board in front of him with somewhat difficult to read, northern-style runes. "The simple matter is that I do not have the strength for such a thing. I am one Shardkeeper already set against three, those remaining who were foolish enough to believe I would help them conquer my homeland. I will not last long against eleven. My intentions are to protect this Republic and thwart the invasion of the Southlands."

"So, you would leave the rest of the north in chains?" he said. "Leave them to languish as slaves?"

"I have no love for slavery—I believe I have proven that through deeds," said Marci. "But I am not a Goddess, Mr. Ehrling. What I might wish and what I can do are two different things. Thwart the invasion of the Southlands, and defend the Republic, this will already consume the full scope of my resources—as it is, I will need funding in order to just accomplish those two objectives."

There were mutters from the gallery, not all of them happy. Marci grimaced; she hated being forced into being a weasel, into behaving like a politician. But she couldn't publicly state her intentions—and actually fuck Mr. Ehrling: either he was a fool who thought she had the strength to battle all the other Shardkeepers at once, or else he was dragging her under the cart for his own political ambitions. She needed to maintain 'strategic ambiguity;' her successful defeat of Callum had taught her the value of no one being entirely sure of her goals.

"So, you expect tribute?" pressed Ehrling.

There were a few angry shouts from the gallery, although not all of them seemed to be cross with Marci, thankfully.

"Tribute is something extracted under threat," snapped Marci, losing her temper. "I have not, am not, and will not threaten the Republic."

"But if you don't get it, you withdraw your protection?" he said.

"How am I supposed to pay my soldiers without income?" said Marci. "My legion of fairies are paid for by Eladraine, yes, but my demon soldiers—the bulk of my forces, particularly after taking over Callum's army—are employed under contracts that will be rendered void if I cannot pay them. If I cannot pay them, then I cannot fight the Shardkeepers who are almost certain to try and invade the Republic."

"Forgive me, Ms. Du Valmont, but that sounds like a 'protection racket.' Perhaps you are simply more intelligent than Callum, and realise that direct rule is messy and inefficient, and that indirect rule is preferable," he said, before pausing for a brief moment. "You strike me as rather intelligent, Ms. Du Valmont."

That got outraged shouts from the gallery, most of them thankfully directed at him. The Chairwoman also seemed less than impressed.

"And you strike me as a fucking idiot," snapped Marci before she could stop herself. "Are you really so dumb that—"

"Ms. Du Valmont, decorum, please; Citizen Ehrling, we are here to ask Ms. Du Valmont questions, not make accusations as to her character," said Ms. Lundin, cutting Marci off as the gallery rang with several guffaws. "If you do not have anything further to ask, I will take the floor from you."

"Nothing further at the moment, no," he said, sitting down. "I cede the floor."

He would be one to watch, thought Marci, clamping down on her not particularly diplomatic anger. She had spent enough time in her mother's court to recognise ambition when she saw it. She didn't want to interfere with the internal politics of the Republic, but she very much hoped he wouldn't end up with some important role after the constitution had been written and then the planned elections had been held.


A.N. I have a Patreon with early chapters, and several other stories in my profile, both original and fanfiction.

Princess of Darkness

The Hellfire Club was nothing like it had been two weeks earlier. Back then, despite the Shardkeeper's constant skirmishes with one another, the atmosphere had been jovial, collegial, with a sense that it was all just a great game. None of them had killed each other, after all. Death was for other people; lesser people.

That atmosphere was gone. When Marci arrived, flanked by twenty heavily armed fairies from the Order of the Verdant Blossom and the biggest, meanest, and toughest winged demons in her employ, the waiter at the door trembled as she ushered her in with a "this way, your Dread Majesty."

Saoirse, Olaf, Raffety, Jolanda, and the usual demons Maeve and Finnley—who had found roles in her army as a lieutenant and a drill sergeant, respectively—had been barred from attending, with Marci taking only crack troops who could fly as fast as she could for if things went south.

She would have preferred to not go at all, but Olaf and Saoirse had convinced her that it was too useful an occasion to pass up. It was the only chance she had to try and gauge the other Shardkeeper's reactions to her, and to try and make sure they didn't form into a unified block against her.

It would mean once again having to play what she was increasingly thinking of as 'Crown Princess Marcelle,' a ruthless, cunning, and vicious fairy who her mother would have loved to have as a daughter. A mask, hiding the somewhat insecure, rebellious, and kinder Marci who she liked to believe was her true self.

Lately, however, it had seemed she had been wearing the mask of a ruthless schemer more often than not. That worried her. How long did it take for a mask to fuse to the skin beneath? How long could she pretend to be a ruthless warlord before she actually became one when so much outside pressure was pushing her in that direction?

There were some demons on the lower levels of the lounge, but only those who were willing to risk getting annihilated in the crossfire of Shardkeeper combat for the off chance of getting some juicy gossip. The fact that there were a dozen airships, armed with cannons and bearing the livery of the Infernal Council hovering all around the building did little to make it feel safer.

Marci hadn't really thought of using airships for warfare. Was there a reason Shardkeepers didn't have them? She knew they were a relatively recent development in the Underworld, and, yes, they were far less resilient than the floating fortresses of doom, but it seemed like a pretty good idea to put cannons on them. That was something she needed to look into. Immediately, even; she sent Rafferty a mental message to please prepare a report on them for her.

The other Shardkeepers had also brought large retinues to their usual spot on the top floor of the club. They were silent, and glared at Marci from their places at the huge round table that they were all sat at, and which had a single space left for her.

"So, the betrayer decides to join us," said Deirdre, her gooey face contorting into a look of hatred. She had been one of the three other demons, apart from Callum, who had been part of the 'coalition' to invade and carve up the south.

"You have some nerve," said Angus, the incubus who with his twin sister Aoife had rounded out the quartet—or quintet, if Marci were counted. He was wearing a fishnet top and startlingly tight pants, with a weird spiky mantle and heavy makeup around the eyes that, honestly, sort of worked for Marci. She might have been with Olaf, but that didn't mean she couldn't appreciate beauty—even the evil sort.

"After you fucking murdered Callum," spat Aoife. She was wearing a far less daring black dress, and of the three looked the most furious. Her eyes were slightly red and puffy—had she been… crying? Damn. That almost made Marci feel bad. Almost.

"Oh, please," said Marci, projecting cool confidence even if inside she was trembling like a toddler whose mother was yelling at her. "You act like you wouldn't have done the same in my stead. I thought we Shardkeepers prided ourselves on our pragmatism? I had the opportunity to make myself stronger, and to take the entire Southlands as my domain. Which of you wouldn't have done the same?"

"I told you she would betray us!" spat Fiona, the small imp who had been the only Shardkeeper to suffer a major defeat in the last war—at the hands of Eladraine's elite aerial troops, as well as being the only Shardkeeper who had immediately clocked Marci for what she really was. The imp levelled a red finger at Deirdre. "I fucking told you!"

"I'd hardly call the reception you received from the Kaiser 'taking the Southlands as your domain,'" scoffed Seamus, a spiny demon who was the jolliest of the Shardkeepers, although now his sharp face was more serious, and while there was a smile there, it didn't reach his eyes.

"Only if you lack imagination," said Marci. "Your problem, all of your problems really, is that you think that the only form of power is crushing domination; power is something new to you, you don't have the…" Marci channelled her best Queen Adele, gave them a toothy smile and tried not to retch, "breeding."

The demons glanced at each other, some annoyed, some thoughtful.

"My family have dominated the Southlands economically for over a millennium; what you neuvau, would-be-monarchs fail to understand is that soft power is often both more durable, and less costly. They might be stroppy about it, but they all know who the real power in the south is."

That wasn't true in the slightest. The Kaiser and his court were out of their wildes-damned minds, and were seemingly actively trying to worsen their relationship. But that would make sense to these demons—or, at least, she hoped it would. After all, the truth, that the real Marci didn't actually want power, and wanted to liberate the Northlands for its own sake, would be even less believable—and potentially more terrifying—than the idea that she was just another ruthless monster.

"If you think we are just going to forget how you looked us in the eye and lied, and just let you take what is ours," spat Deirdre, "then you are delusional, Princess."

"And you are foolish if you think that won't end the same way it did for Callum," said Marci. "Shall I tell my kobolds to start making preparations to redo your Shardfort's decor? Or are you going to do the smart thing and count your lucky stars you weren't the lamb I led to slaughter above Krefeld an Nain?"

The slime-demon visibly flinched, and a tense silence fell over the table. Marci gave her hands something to do to stop them trembling, picking up the menu that had been placed in front of her seat and pretending to peruse it even as she withdrew her focus slightly and pushed it into her other body, located within the Dark Bulwark, and which had a helpfully placed pillow ready to scream into.

"How did you do it?"

The question came from Isolde, a half-human half-succubus woman who looked basically elvish. She commanded the Crowntaker, and was the quietest of all the Shardkeepers. From what Marci knew from the reports that had been prepared for her on all the other Shardkeepers, she knew Isolde ruled the far northern region of Ursland, and had also settled a few previously uninhabited islands in the Frozen Sea that now produced great quantities of metal. She was the most defensive of the Shardkeepers, and most focused on the fortification and economic development of her realm. She didn't really engage in offensive action, and instead had maintained a non-aggressive posture with her four abutting Shardkeepers that more or less held fast.

"Do what?" said Marci.

"How did you purge Callum's soul without destroying the Shard?" continued Isolde in a soft voice. "It wasn't the blast from that weapon of yours. You still had to fight aboard. The blast merely weakened him somehow."

Marci wasn't surprised to know that she had agents in Krefeld. They all must have.

"You don't really expect me to answer that, do you?" said Marci.

Isolde pursed her lips.

"Fundamentally," said Marci, taking her other face out from the pillow back on the Dark Bulwark and picking up a pre-written card with a few options with tags such as 'more evil,' and 'more conciliatory.' "Nothing needs to change. So long as you stay out of my domains, Kattlandia and the Southlands, we will get along just fine. I am not an unreasonable fairy, I simply take exception to those trying to… how did you put it, Deirdre? Ah yes, 'trying to take what is mine.'"

A few of the Shardkeepers around the table visibly relaxed, and Marci allowed one of the knots of tension located where her wings met her back to also unwind slightly. This was all she had to accomplish here today—make some of them think better of unifying against her. Sow doubt in the idea that she was coming for them all.

Which she was. She was going to kill each and every single Shardkeeper in this room. They couldn't be allowed to live, or, more specifically, their Shardforts couldn't be allowed to keep on weakening the defences of the world against the Far Ones. If she found a way to sever them from their Shards without killing them, a technique she hoped to find eventually for herself, she wasn't opposed to the idea of using it, but, for the moment, she was plotting to kill each and every one of them.

Did that make her a psychopath? It did seem like something her mother would do…

The atmosphere began to slowly thaw after that, although Deirdre, Aoife, and Angus all left in disgust before dinner arrived.

Marci had some kind of 'mushroom risotto,' which was some weird demon dish that included rice, cheese, and several different types of fungi. It came with a wine accompaniment that Marci declined automatically. That, at least, seemed to be something she had under control. She didn't have time to drink.

Although, then again, given that she was a disembodied consciousness, and she'd only be affected by alcohol's effects embodying herself in that body, perhaps that wasn't even the victory she thought it was. Stupid abominable eldritch artefact that housed her soul, she couldn't even really take pride in the fact that she'd managed to get sober.

"So, Princess," said Enya, the four-armed, purple furred wrath demon who was sitting on her left and who commanded 'Inferno Peak.' "Perhaps it is a bit gauche to say so soon, but I do believe congratulations are in order."

Marci almost spat out her sparkling water.

"What?" she said.

"A masterstroke, really," continued Enya, raising her crystal wine flute to Marci and giving her a conspiratorial wink. "However it was you did it. We all took you for a minnow, a little girl out of her depth—it turns out you were the biggest shark here all along."

Marci was, for a moment, stunned. She had come here expecting to face universal hostility, with victory looking like a still angry but not unified array of Shardkeepers. She hadn't been expecting alliance overtures. Well, that might be too strong, but Enya was—despite knowing that Marci was a backstabber—trying to get on her good side.

These people were out of their infernal minds.

"My holdings lie on the other side of Deirdre's, as I'm sure you're aware," said Enya. "If she gives your little 'Republic' trouble, feel free to let me know, hmm? She has this marvellous little area with vineyards I've been dying to get my hands on. Never pass up an opportunity, yes?"

Absolutely nuts.

"I'll… ah, remember that," said Marci.



***



The rest of the 'soiree' passed without much incident, and Marci excused herself after the dessert course. She made for the airship dock feeling exhausted. Still, she had gotten through the meeting, driven a wedge between the remaining survivors of the Southern Invasion Coalition and the rest of the Shardkeepers, and even received some shaky offers of quasi-alliances. Not that she could trust those like Enya any further than they could trust her. They were, all of them, just out for their own interests.

Still, she was surprised when, just as she was about to board Callum's old airship. A voice addressed her from her left.

"A moment, Princess."

Marci looked sideways, frowning when she saw Isolde—the half-succubus, half-human woman who had questioned her once during the 'meeting' section of the soiree. After that, she hadn't said anything, and must have slipped away. Come to think of it, this was probably only the third time Marci had ever heard her speak: once when she had introduced herself; once when she had asked her question, and now.

"Yes?" said Marci.

"Here," said Isolde, holding out a letter in crisp, expensive looking paper sealed with light blue wax. "Read this once you are back aboard your Shardfort. It will combust if you open it beforehand."

Marci hesitantly accepted the letter and cast a quick scanning charm. It did indeed have an enchantment on it, a rather simple one that would destroy the contents if it was opened before being exposed to some kind of complex magical frequency that looked like it might have something to do with the Shardkeeper portals—psionic energy, certainly.

"Why?" asked Marci. "What does it say?"

Isolde said nothing, merely inclined her head and then turned, walking back into the club. Marci watched her go, and then did another three inspections of the letter—only to find not so much as a skerrick of magic beyond the charm designed to destroy the contents if opened early. It was also very well done magic, and Marci wasn't sure she'd actually be able to break it without triggering the fail-safe even if she really, really, really tried.

Her attention remained on the letter for the short trip back to the portal nexus, and she barely heard Captain Valetta as the woman asked her something about security, giving her a vague answer to 'take it up with Rafferty.'

Sure enough, as soon as she passed through the portal back to the Dark Bulwark, the enchantment on the letter unwove itself, leaving her with a totally unenchanted envelope.

She tore it open, frowning when she saw two items inside.

The first, a cheque for a frankly stupid amount of money with a demonic bank, made out to her and from some very generic sounding company: 'Frostward Holdings LLC.' It was, while not as much money as she had seized from Callum's treasury, still enough to, by itself, pay Callum's forces for several months. Why the fuck had Isolde, another Shardkeeper, given her that? Without any kind of agreement, even?

She turned to the second item, a note folded in half and written in neat, if somewhat stilted Eladrainese.



We seem to have much more in common than I first realised. Meet one of my employees at the Viper's Nest in Dis at 8pm (6pm Pandemonium Time) next Fourthday. Come as a trusted low-profile employee, not yourself, and say you're there to see a 'Crowley.' I have already made the reservation.



Marci spent several long moments staring at the letter, trying to figure out what the fuck was going on. A proposal for Alliance, certainly, but why all the secrecy? None of the others seemed that bothered by being obvious that they were manoeuvring—even with Callum's death, it all remained game-like. And Isolde? Marci knew nothing about the Shardkeeper, had never spoken to her one on one before that night. Beyond the fact she controlled a large swathe of the far north, and that she was regarded as the most defensive of all the Shardkeepers, she had next to no information on her.

"Crown Princess!? May I beg a moment of your time?"

The thought came from a fairy who she had dispatched as a liaison for the Eladraine Embassy which was still unpacking in Krefeld an Nain beneath.

"What is it?" replied Marci, perhaps a tad more sharply than she should have.

"We have a problem, your highness; it concerns your agents Ms. Tissa and Lady Duin."

Interlude: Tissa

"So, um, this seems nice?" said Saoirse, looking around at the Dancing Duke, one of the public houses in Krefeld an Nain that Tissa frequented when in the city. It was a little bit upmarket, but it had the most wonderful sticky date pudding. So, when Saoirse had asked if she'd 'like to have, um, a drink with me' Tissa had known exactly where to go.

The succubus was wearing a glamour, disguising her horns, tail, wings, and red eyes and making her appear elvish. Tissa had offered to go to a tavern in Pandemonium instead, since she didn't want her friend to be uncomfortable or feel like she had to be deceptive—Tissa would have found that most distressing—but Saoirse had said she'd 'like to see more of your world.'

The large two-story space had fewer patrons than the last time that Tissa had visited, and they were able to get a nice table on the balcony overlooking the park that you usually had to book for. It was still a bit chilly in early spring, but the noon sun made it pleasant.

"We would like four stick-date puddings, please," said Tissa to the waiter, who she remembered from her last visit—an older gentleman who for some reason had sighed when he'd seen her entering the establishment, stooping a little to get through the human sized-door. "And also a vanilla milkshake, a mocha coffee, a pint of the Blackbrook ale, a bowl of roast potatoes, and a twenty-ounce steak, extra-rare, thank-you."

"And would the lady like those blended into a bowl?" asked the waiter. "Or perhaps ground into a fine paste?"

"No, we would like them separate please!" said Tissa with a laugh. "Is that a new trend in the city? We find the thought of such a thing a little unseemly!"

"Quite," said the waiter, who also apparently didn't think much of the idea. "And for you, Lady elf?"

"I will please have the pudding," said Saoirse in her ever-improving Altisch, a deep frown on her face. "And water please, thank-you."

"Of course," said the waiter, making a note before moving off.

"We like it here," said Tissa. "We would be glad to show Friend-Saoirse more of the city too, if she likes?"

"Um, yes, I would like that," said Saoirse, turning and looking at the waiter.

"Oh, did you wish to order something else?" asked Tissa.

"No, it's just… he wasn't very nice to you," said Saoirse.

"Wasn't he?" said Tissa, cocking her head to one side. "We do find it hard to tell sometimes—Altlanders rarely say things in a straightforward manner. We find it most vexing."

"Yes, he… he was making fun of you," nodded Saoirse, biting her lip. "I'm sorry, that's awful of him. You're such a wonderful person."

"Our thanks! We are gratified and pleased to hear that."

Friend-Saoirse had gotten dressed up, perhaps overdressed for the occasion, even, wearing the same rather nice red jacket and white cravat she had worn to the quite disastrous meeting of Marci and the Kaiser, along with some red lipstick. Tissa had been going to tell her she should probably wear just one of her normal cardigans, but then she had remembered Anke telling her to 'keep your opinions on fashion to yourself,' and she hadn't wanted to upset her Succubus friend.

"Tissa," she said. "I, uh, I'm not very good at this…"

"Eating pudding?" said Tissa. "We assure you, Friend-Saoirse, it isn't difficult. Do demons—"

She caught herself and shook her head. Friend-Saoirse was pretending to be an elf. Untruths were hard to remember, and even if understandable in this context, a little bit dishonourable…

"Do elves, of which Friend-Saoirse is one, not have pudding?"

"No, ah, I mean…"

"Hey, aren't you that lizard that hangs around with that demon-lover?"

The voice came from a table over, and Tissa initially ignored them. Saoirse, however, turned to face them, an angry look on her face. Ah, 'lizard,' yes—that was what incorrect people often referred to Arana as.

"Hello," said Tissa, turning towards a quartet of young men who had all chosen to seat themselves at the table directly next to Tissa and Saoirse. Which made sense, this area had the best view, and was not partially blocked from the sun by a large tree. "Assuming you are speaking to us, we are unsure to whom you are referring by 'demon-lover.'"

"That fairy," said one of them, a rather well-dressed man with a fancy looking sword at his hip. "Marcelle du Valmont."

"Ah!" said Tissa, nodding. "Yes, Dear-Friend Marci is our dear friend!"

"Ugh, revolting," said another of the young men. "The Kaiser should have had her hung; what a disgusting traitor."

Tissa stilled. "Please do not speak about our Dear-Friend like that," said Tissa.

"Or what?" sneered one of the men, standing up and putting a hand on the hilt of his sword. "What are you going to do about it, you reptile freak? You a demon lover too?"

"We are going to strenuously object to your hurtful characterisations and suggest that you are not a very nice person," said Tissa. "Although, we will admit that we cannot be absolute sure after such a short interaction. And while we do not know precisely what you mean by 'demon-lover,' we know several demons who are very nice people."

The quartet of humans looked at each other. From their tense body language, it seemed like they were expecting something. What, exactly, she wasn't sure.

"You are a dishonourable cur!" shouted one of them.

"That is untrue and hurtful," said Tissa. "We believe we were correct in our initial assessment as to your unkind character. We would politely request you find another table to sit at."

"Oh, are you going to make us?" said another.

"No," said Tissa. "Although we believe it would make for a far more enjoyable dining experience for both of groups."

The four men looked at each other.

"Oh, who fucking cares if she starts it?" said one of them, drawing his sword. "Get her!"

Tissa wasn't very good at reading human social cues and customs, or those of elves or dwarves or fairies, really, even after living in their lands for almost twenty years. But she recognised violence, and those about to commit it. They had drawn steel with intention; they meant to murder her. So, as the men's drew their blades, she reacted in a most reasonable way: she reached under the table, gasped one of the legs, and then hurled the heavy wooden object directly at them.

The large, heavy wooden table hit the leader head on, and clipped a second, breaking something with a crack.

The other two swore and lunged for her. Tissa, however, was a warrior of the Arana; she had trained with the blade since she had chosen the path at the tender age of twelve, and she could see dozens of flaws in their movements, stances, and postures at a glance.

Tissa stepped towards them, one hand reaching back to draw her double-headed glaive, the other pulling a knife from her belt and throwing it reverse-grip and underhand in a fluid movement straight at the human on the left—a red haired man with a scar on one cheek that looked to have been inflicted with what she would guess had been a rapier. The weapon whizzed forward, taking him in his sword arm and making him scream in pain and drop his blade.

The other closed on her, but she parried his weapon with her tail blade which, while wrapped in cloth, was still capable of deflection. She finished drawing her glaive, and she brought it down in a purposeful, but non-lethal sweep, cutting through the man's wrists and rendering him less dangerous.

The human man screamed and looked down at his severed wrists in horror for a moment before she kicked him in the chest, sending him careening back across the restaurant towards where his two fellows who she'd hit with the table were recovering.

"What the fuck—"

Tissa danced forward, towards the one she had clipped, and who was still holding a weapon. He saw her coming, and managed to get his weapon into a defensive posture. His guard, however, was too high to be fighting an Arana armed with a tail blade, and she bound his sabre with her glaive and then stabbed him in the leg with her now mostly revealed tail-blade. He screamed and staggered, and she capitalised on his distraction to twist her glaive around his crossguard and bring the blade through his hand, severing his fingers and sending his weapon clattering to the ground before she leveraged her weapon around and smacked him with the flat of the other blade in the side of the head hard enough that he crumpled sideways, bleeding and probably concussed, but not dead.

Three rendered pacific, one to go.

The last of them, the leader stood and regarded her with a pale face. He fumbled for his belt, where he had a flintlock pistol. Tissa raised her weapon to protect her face, and was about to charge him when a blast of dark energy picked him up and hurled him off the balcony—courtesy of Friend-Saoirse.

Tissa's eyes flicked back to the man who she had stuck in the arm with a knife, who had fallen against a table and was screaming. Before she could move to disarm him, however, there was a rushing of boots, and she looked back to the door that led to the restaurant proper to see dozens of heavily armed city guard rushing in.

"Oh, good," said Tissa. "These men attacked us—"

"Drop your weapons, and put your hands on your head!"
